# LITs with `tags` `philosophy-of-technology`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Philosophy of technology** — what technology is and what it does to those who live with it — the autonomy of technique, technological determinism and the social shaping of technology, lock-in and practical compulsion, automation and deskilling, technical codes and the politics of artifacts, design that steers or captures its users, critical theory of technology and convivial tools. A technology's regulation stays with society-and-governance, a measured effect of one product with social-science and a verdict on what is owed with ethics, unless the work argues about technology as such; how software is built is software-engineering (group: philosophy; ADR-098).

| [LIT-1002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1002.md) v4 | Technology, autonomy, and manipulation | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum (2019), Internet Policy Review 8(2). Manipulation is hidden influence: intentionally and covertly influencing someone's decision-making by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities, where covert means the target is not and could not easily become aware of it. Surveillance, adaptive interfaces and the habitual invisibility of technology make it easy. Its harm is to autonomy, in both competency and authenticity, and beneficent manipulation carries it too; the paper claims a harm in every case, not that manipulation is always wrong. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md)) in full; worth reading for the standard statement of the covert-influence view: manipulation is "intentionally and covertly influencing their decision-making, by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities", with attempted covertness as its mark, and for the argument that its harm is to autonomy and is carried even by beneficent manipulation, through the target's opacity to herself. Read it knowing that it is a short policy essay, that the definition is stipulated and its intent requirement never examined, that it excludes manipulation of institutions and never considers manipulation by them, and that it claims a harm in every case, not a wrong. |
| [LIT-1297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1297.md) v2 | The End of Ownership: Personal Property in the Digital Economy | Perzanowski and Schultz (2016). Digital media and software-laden devices are sold under licences that deny a sale and DRM that enforces the licence, while the law of exhaustion, built around owning a tangible copy, cannot follow purchases that are copied at every use or never copied at all. Buyers lose resale, lending, repair and privacy, and a survey shows "Buy Now" misleads them. The book proposes treating one-time purchases as sales, judging licences as permissions rather than contracts, exempting owners from anti-circumvention law, and a multifactor test for digital exhaustion. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1026.md)) in full except the last page of the Conclusion, which the copy lacks; worth reading as the standard account of how licences, DRM and the copy-centred law of exhaustion turn digital purchases into conditional access, with the case law from Bobbs-Merrill to Lexmark v. Impression Products, a survey showing that "Buy Now" misleads buyers, and a proposed multifactor test for digital exhaustion. Its diagnosis is the consumer side of Lessig's copy trigger: exhaustion is tied to owning a copy, and digital use and transfer make new copies. Read it knowing that it is US law as of early 2016, that it is advocacy by two authors who were parties or counsel in several of its episodes, that the survey is their own and of a mock store, and that several of its pending cases have since been decided. |

| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) v2 | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |

A theoretical perspective with no data of its own; its aviation evidence, chiefly Casner et al. (2014), is reported second-hand, without samples, sizes or horizons; and its claim that AI assistants accelerate decay beyond automation is a hypothesis it says no research has tested. |

| [LIT-2560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2560.md) v4 | One-Dimensional Man: Studies in the Ideology of Advanced Industrial Society | Herbert Marcuse (1964). One-Dimensional Man. Beacon Press. Read in full ([NOTE-1924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1924.md)). Advanced industrial society contains qualitative change by satisfying needs it has itself produced, "false" needs "superimposed upon the individual by particular social interests in his repression": a "comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom" secured by "Technology rather than Terror", in which "Domination is transfigured into administration". The apparatus's impersonality veils the interests that choose a society's project, and its administrators are enclosed by it too. It bounds [CLAIM-682](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-682.md), because control through a veiled project is not discretion over the dependent, not because no one holds it ([ARG-109](../../../record/arguments.d/ARG-109.md)); it corroborates [CLAIM-677](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-677.md)'s mechanism and argues against its measure, "what can be chosen and what is chosen" ([ARG-108](../../../record/arguments.d/ARG-108.md)). Account: [THEORY-1853](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1853.md). | Active — read in full on 2026-11-13 from the whole book posted chapter by chapter on the Marcuse family's site, https://www.marcuse.org/herbert/pubs/64onedim/ (contents, Introduction, chapters 1 to 10), on the owner's ruling of 2026-11-13 that the whole-book copies named here are fine to read ("the copies are fine"). An OCR transcription; quotations follow it. Read in [NOTE-1924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1924.md); account [THEORY-1853](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1853.md). Farr's SEP entry ([LIT-2589](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2589.md)) stood in before. |

Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (PB2019-101402). The NTSB found the probable cause to be the operator's failure to monitor the road and the automated system, through distraction by her phone. Uber ATG's inadequate risk assessment, operator oversight and countermeasures to automation complacency, "all a consequence of its inadequate safety culture", contributed, as did the impaired pedestrian's crossing and Arizona's oversight. The system was designed to rely on the operator to avoid collisions, and ATG's culture contributed to the operator's distraction itself. The report disclaims fault and blame. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2034.md), [THEORY-1932](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1932.md)). | [LIT-2665](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2665.md) v3 | Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction | Elish (2019). Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction. Engaging Science, Technology, and Society 5: 40-60. DOI 10.17351/ests2019.260. Elish names the moral crumple zone: when control over an automated system is distributed, responsibility for its failure can be misattributed to the nearest human operator, who had limited control, so that the operator absorbs moral and legal blame and "the integrity of the technological system" is protected. She argues it from the reception of Three Mile Island and Air France 447, through media framing, certification and the operator's legal final authority, and expects it of self-driving cars. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2019](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2019.md), [THEORY-1928](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1928.md)). Argues, with Watson's and Shoemaker's accountability, attributability and answerability, that AI decision support threatens responsibility chiefly as attributability: a decision made with a tool that presupposes outcome-shaping values the user has not endorsed is hers in name but does not express her value-judgements. The gap comes in degrees and descriptive tools open it too; remedies are endorsement through transparency, value calibration and confining tools to description. Read; the reading is [NOTE-2007](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2007.md) and [THEORY-1915](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1915.md). | [LIT-2684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2684.md) | Contestable AI by Design: Towards a Framework | Alfrink, Keller, Kortuem and Doorn (2022; Minds and Machines 33(4): 613-639, 2023). A systematic review and thematic synthesis of the contestable-AI literature into a design framework of five system features (built-in safeguards, interactive control, explanations, human review and intervention requests, tools for scrutiny) and six development practices (ex-ante safeguards, agonistic ML development, QA during and after development, risk mitigation, third-party oversight). Contestability should run through the lifecycle: before a decision takes effect through safeguards, control and ex-ante contestation of design choices, and after it through review, since subjects' intervention requests are "necessarily post-hoc". Untested. Read 2026-11-16 as a partial stand-in for Harid (2026), [LIT-2676](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2676.md), for the concept of contestability before execution only. In a Pólya-urn model of predictive policing that learns only from incidents its own patrols discover, deployment converges on the region that started ahead when crime rates are equal and on the higher-rate region however slight the difference when they are not; reported incidents attenuate but do not remove the effect; discarding discovered incidents in proportion to patrol probability restores convergence to the true rates. | [LIT-2689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2689.md) v3 | Positioning public sector practitioners as 'moral crumple zones': Mechanisms in the early use of generative AI work support tools | Choroszewicz (2026). Positioning public sector practitioners as 'moral crumple zones': Mechanisms in the early use of generative AI work support tools. Government Information Quarterly 43(2): 102128. DOI 10.1016/j.giq.2026.102128. From 2.5 years of ethnography of generative-AI tool trials in two Finnish public organizations, the author finds test users positioned as moral crumple zones. They were held responsible for the quality, verification and use of outputs from immature, opaque tools they could not shape, and poor outputs were framed as user error. Five mechanisms produce this: oversight and liability taken for granted, immature tools marketed as "sparring buddies", trial-and-error learning offloaded to users, limited transparency, and a burden of vigilance. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2032](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2032.md), [THEORY-1916](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1916.md)). It corroborates the allocation clause of [CLAIM-707](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-707.md); it observes prospective allocation, not blame after a harm. | [LIT-2691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2691.md) v3 | Agency Laundering and Information Technologies | Rubel, Castro and Pham (2021). Agency Laundering and Information Technologies. Algorithms and Autonomy: The Ethics of Automated Decision Systems (Cambridge University Press), ch. 7, pp. 137–162. DOI 10.1017/9781108895057.007. Defines agency laundering as a wrong of accountability: a party responsible for a domain makes a process, person or technology partly causally responsible for outcomes in it, ascribes it morally relevant qualities, obscures its own causal role, and so forestalls others' demands for an account, even while meeting its substantive role responsibilities. Facebook's ad categories, Uber's surge prompts and Houston's EVAAS firings launder; Uber's goal reminders and the Loomis court's use of COMPAS do not. Distinguished from responsibility gaps, bias laundering and masking; humans in the loop can launder too. The book version of [LIT-2659](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2659.md). | [LIT-2696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2696.md) v3 | Discussion Paper on Agentic A.I. Governance in the Banking Sector | Hong Kong Monetary Authority (2026). Discussion Paper on Agentic A.I. Governance in the Banking Sector. November 2026 (file of 2 November). A non- binding discussion paper. The HKMA proposes "intent-anchored accountability": an AI agent in a bank should act only for an approved business intent, within delegated authority that is defined in advance, technically enforced through an "agent harness" (least-privilege permissions, deterministic checks, transaction and velocity limits, approval gates) and changed only through change control, with a named accountable owner. Human oversight (in, on or "in command" of the loop) counts only where effective. A formal approval step is not oversight when volume or velocity outruns review ("approval fatigue"). Intervention is designed around detection, decision and stopping time so that it comes before harm becomes irreversible. Where oversight cannot keep pace, the agent's authority, scope or velocity should be cut. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2018](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2018.md), [THEORY-1931](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1931.md)). It is the documentary source of the standing- constraint architecture in [CLAIM-711](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-711.md), corroborates [CLAIM-705](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-705.md) qualitatively, and bears on [QUESTION-471](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-471.md) and [TERM-125](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-125.md). | [LIT-2699](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2699.md) | Fewer Burdens but Greater Inequality? Reevaluating the Safety Net through the Lens of Administrative Burden | Herd and Moynihan (2023). The ANNALS of the American Academy of Political and Social Science 706: 94–117. Over the past 30 years administrative burden (learning, compliance and psychological costs of claiming benefits) fell on average in the large US means-tested programs (EITC, SNAP, Medicaid under the ACA), with rising take-up, while inequality in who bears burdens grew through federalism, the tax system and privatization. Burdens restrict access to rights and benefits, fall on those with less power, and are constructed, sometimes deliberately, as policymaking by other means. Read as a stand-in for [LIT-2660](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2660.md). | Active |
| [LIT-2701](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2701.md) v2 | The Paradox of Algorithms and Blame on Public Decision-makers | Ozer, Waggoner and Kennedy (2024). The Paradox of Algorithms and Blame on Public Decision-makers. Business and Politics 26(2): 200–217. DOI 10.1017/bap.2023.35. Two pre-registered vignette experiments on three representative US samples test whether algorithms shield public decision-makers from blame. A judge whose probation decision ends in a death is blamed no less for following an algorithm and not uniquely more for rejecting it; advice of any kind slightly raises blame, the algorithm is blamed without lowering the judge's share, and the rise for following it is mostly mediated by perceived abdication. Effects are small and fade in the third sample. | [LIT-2704](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2704.md) | Effective Voice: Beyond Exit and Affect in Online Communities | Frey and Schneider (2020). Drawing on Hirschman, they distinguish affective voice (expression that seeks to persuade power holders) from effective voice (speech with a binding effect through transparent processes) and argue that online platforms make exit and affective voice cheap while effective voice is nearly absent and control is consolidated. They propose mechanisms: rules binding on administrators, selection and removal of those in authority, binding petition thresholds, internal blocs and designed occasions for structural change. | Active |
| [LIT-2705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2705.md) v3 | Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account | Santoni de Sio and van den Hoven (2018). Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account. Frontiers in Robotics and AI 5: 15. DOI 10.3389/frobt.2018.00015. Grounds the autonomous-weapons principle of meaningful human control in Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control: a system is under such control only if it tracks the relevant moral reasons of the humans who design and deploy it, and the relevant facts, and its behaviour traces to at least one human who understands its capabilities and that its effects will be attributed to them. Presence in the loop is not sufficient; tracing can carry responsibility upstream from an operator to designers and to whoever, like Kamm's captain, is the "choice architect"; control is necessary, not sufficient, for good conduct. Sketched for automated driving. Read; the reading is [NOTE-2024](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2024.md) and [THEORY-1939](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1939.md). | [LIT-2707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2707.md) | "Making Out" While Driving: Relational and Efficiency Games in the Gig Economy | Cameron (2022), Organization Science 33(1): 231-252. Four years of fieldwork with ride-hail drivers (participant observation, 136 interviews with 63 drivers) find that, without managers or coworkers, drivers make their work meaningful through two workplace games: a relational game scored by the app's customer ratings, in which the platform appears as a facilitator and drivers follow its suggestions, and an efficiency game tracked with their own tools and sometimes by manipulating the algorithm, in which it appears as an opponent. Both produce engagement; the paper does not claim they produce consent. Read 2026-11-16 as a partial stand-in for Cameron (2024), [LIT-2686](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2686.md): same fieldwork, the precursor of its two tactics, not its concepts of constant and confined choices or choice-based consent. In a simulated hiring screen on census data, four upstream choices (label definition, feature measurement, model-selection metric, validation strategy) are varied; three move the counterfactual explanations given to rejected candidates more than the explanation method's own validity threshold does.
